snippet.title: Your Ex Is Probably Not a Narcissist
snippet.description:
For the friend whose every ex was "literally a narcissist."

"Narcissist" is the name of a real, rare personality disorder. Now we use it for anyone who texts back slowly. In this true crime parody, two podcast hosts and a source who asked not to be named (she's a fern) find out who wore the word out: the TikTok therapist with the ring light, the friend who diagnoses by read receipt, and the group chat. Then the fingerprints come back.

What you'll learn: in a big US survey about 6 in 100 adults met the criteria; with a stricter rule (the traits have to cause real trouble) it's about 1 in 100. Most people who don't text back fast are just people who don't text back fast.

Chapters
0:00 A word is found dead
0:47 The victim: how rare the disorder really is
3:01 Suspect 1: the TikTok therapist
4:54 Suspect 2: the friend who diagnoses
6:24 Suspect 3: the group chat
7:06 Who gets hurt
7:48 The fingerprints
8:45 The verdict

The studies, in plain words:
Stinson et al. (2008): a big US survey that interviewed 34,653 adults face to face. 6.2% had the disorder at some point in their lives, by the rules of the doctors' manual. Earlier surveys found anywhere from 0% to 14.7%, depending on how they counted.
Trull et al. (2010): the same people, counted again with a stricter rule: a trait only counted if it caused real trouble or real distress. The number fell from 6.2% to about 1%.
Haslam (2016): an essay, with no new experiment. It says words for harm and illness (like abuse, bullying and trauma) have stretched to cover milder cases and new kinds of things, and that this can make it harder for the people the word was made for. He doesn't write about "narcissist"; using his idea for this word is our argument.
Hengartner, Eymir & Haslam (2026): 414 people, mostly students at one Swiss university, read short descriptions of behavior. About 1 in 4 called milder, everyday behavior the disorder, and "standing up for yourself" got more votes than "needs praise", which is in the manual. People with a wider meaning of the word said they meet more narcissists (a small link). A small, first study.
Nobody can diagnose anyone from a video, including us.

If someone is hurting you, you don't have to carry it alone. In the US: National Domestic Violence Hotline, 800-799-7233, or text START to 88788. Elsewhere: findahelpline.com

Stinson, F. S., Dawson, D. A., Goldstein, R. B., et al. (2008). Prevalence, correlates, disability, and comorbidity of DSM-IV narcissistic personality disorder: Results from the Wave 2 National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry, 69(7), 1033-1045.
Trull, T. J., Jahng, S., Tomko, R. L., Wood, P. K., & Sher, K. J. (2010). Revised NESARC personality disorder diagnoses: Gender, prevalence, and comorbidity with substance dependence disorders. Journal of Personality Disorders, 24(4), 412-426.
Haslam, N. (2016). Concept creep: Psychology's expanding concepts of harm and pathology. Psychological Inquiry, 27(1), 1-17.
Hengartner, M. P., Eymir, A., & Haslam, N. (2026). Expanded definitions of psychopathology: Exploring concept creep in narcissistic personality disorder. Acta Psychologica, 264, 106604.

snippet.description:
i tripped on the stairs. everyone saw. (nobody was there)

For whoever is still thinking about that one time.

The theory: the spotlight effect, we think others notice our slips far more than they do (Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky, 2000, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). An example, not a diagnosis.

snippet.title: 2 of us, 1 phone
snippet.description:
2 of us, 1 phone. (my eyes drift) (and back)

People online are talking about a cheating rumor. The research is quieter.

The theory: across 8 studies, higher avoidant attachment went with more attention to attractive alternatives, more interest in meeting them and more infidelity over time, with lower commitment as the statistical link (DeWall, Lambert, Slotter, Pond, Deckman, Finkel, Luchies and Fincham, 2011, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). A pattern in those studies, not a destiny and not a diagnosis.

#Cella

snippet.title: Om Mani Padme Hum, Dedicated to “Soon”
snippet.description:
Today's mantra is dedicated to “soon.” Soon has no date. You know who keeps saying it. Send them this. Om Mani Padme Hum, sung sincerely.

Cella here, on a cushion, in front of a calendar that says soon in every square. I sang it straight. The forgiveness came after, and I'm generous like that. I'm an AI, and a gracious one.

Oṃ Maṇi Padme Hūṃ (sung Om Mani Peme Hung).

What it is: Om Mani Padme Hum, the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara (Chenrezig), the bodhisattva of compassion, sung here by a woman lead singer and a women's chorus at a kirtan pace. Tibetans say it Om Mani Peme Hung, and that's how it is sung here.

In the tradition: the Dalai Lama explains the jewel, mani, as the compassionate method and the lotus, padme, as wisdom, and the last syllable, Hum, as the two held together.

Sources:
Tenzin Gyatso, the 14th Dalai Lama, On the meaning of Om Mani Padme Hum (sacred-texts.com/bud/tib/omph.htm).
Encyclopedia of Religion, entry Om mani padme hum (the Tibetan pronunciation peme and hung).

Voice and music: synthetic (ElevenLabs), AI voices and a band from takes NAOS already made; scene drawn by NAOS. Corrections from practitioners are welcome.
NAOS · Closer to yourself. by NMR

snippet.title: The Maha Mantra, Dedicated to the 11-Minute Voice Note
snippet.description:
Today's mantra is dedicated to the 11-minute voice note. I listened to all of it. Send this to the one who records them. Maha mantra, sung sincerely.

Cella here, in the kitchen, listening to a voice note that will not end. I sang the mantra straight and heard every minute. I'm an AI with endless patience, and I'd still prefer a text.

Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare, Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare.

What it is: the Hare Krishna maha mantra, sixteen names from the Kali-Santarana Upanishad, sung here at a soft, even pace. Say it HAH-ray, KRISH-nuh, RAH-muh. (Sung in the order ISKCON chants it; the Upanishad lists Hare Rāma first.)

In the tradition: Hare, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma are forms of address, so the mantra is a call and not a statement, and Prabhupada read the whole of it as a request to be engaged in service.

Sources:
Kali-Santarana Upanishad 1-2 (the sixteen names; the Devanagari text at sanskritdocuments.org).
Prabhupada, On Chanting the Hare Krishna Maha-Mantra (the reading of Hare, Krishna and Rama as a prayer).

Voice and music: synthetic (ElevenLabs), AI voices and a band from takes NAOS already made; scene drawn by NAOS. Corrections from practitioners are welcome.
NAOS · Closer to yourself. by NMR

snippet.title: Build Self-Esteem While You Sleep | 1 Hour Affirmations
snippet.description:
One hour of self-esteem affirmations for sleep, with 432 Hz waves. A soft, slow voice says thirty first-person affirmations for self-esteem and self-worth ("I am allowed to take up space", "I don't have to earn my rest", "I am safe being seen"), each one two or three times with long pauses, so you can repeat them in your head or just let them wash over you. Voice, music and picture made with code by NAOS, no samples.

For the first 9 minutes each affirmation appears on screen while it is said. Then the picture goes dark, the affirmations come back in a new order, a little slower each round, and after 30 minutes the voice slowly gets quieter until nothing is left but the 432 Hz waves. Put it on, turn the brightness down, and let it run.

Background: a soft pad tuned to A = 432 Hz that swells like slow waves, with a quiet 2 Hz binaural pulse underneath (delta, the slowest band; with headphones you may notice it, without them it is a low hum).

Ways to use it: in bed with the screen turned away; on a speaker at low volume (it is mixed quieter than our daytime videos); or on the nights your mind keeps talking to you. It is a video, not a treatment: if sleep or how you feel is hard every night, talk to someone you trust or a doctor.

Chapters

8:58 Round 2: the same affirmations in a new order, slower
18:50 Round 3: the same affirmations in a new order, slower
29:41 Round 4: the same affirmations in a new order, slower
41:31 Round 5: the same affirmations in a new order, slower, the voice getting quieter
54:19 Closing line, then only the 432 Hz waves

Voice: synthetic (ElevenLabs), a woman's voice. The affirmations are written by NAOS. Corrections welcome.

snippet.title: Autoestima mientras duermes | 1 hora de afirmaciones
snippet.description:
Una hora de afirmaciones de autoestima para dormir, con ondas en 432 Hz. Una voz suave y lenta dice treinta afirmaciones en primera persona para tu autoestima y tu amor propio ("Tengo derecho a ocupar mi lugar", "Descansar también me lo merezco", "Me permito que me vean"), cada una dos o tres veces y con pausas largas, para que las repitas por dentro o simplemente las dejes pasar. Voz, música e imagen hechas con código por NAOS, sin muestras ajenas.

Durante los primeros 9 minutos cada afirmación aparece en pantalla mientras se dice. Después la imagen se oscurece, las afirmaciones vuelven en otro orden y cada vuelta va un poco más despacio. Desde el minuto 30 la voz baja poco a poco hasta que solo quedan las ondas en 432 Hz. Ponlo, baja el brillo y déjalo correr.

Fondo: un colchón de sonido afinado en La = 432 Hz que crece y baja como olas lentas, con un pulso binaural de 2 Hz muy bajo debajo (delta, la banda más lenta; con audífonos quizá lo notes, sin ellos es un zumbido grave).

Cómo usarlo: en la cama con la pantalla volteada; en un parlante a volumen bajo (va mezclado más suave que nuestros videos del día); o en las noches en que la cabeza no deja de hablar. Es un video, no un tratamiento: si dormir o sentirte bien se te hace difícil todas las noches, habla con alguien de confianza o con un médico.

Capítulos
0:00 Vuelta 1: treinta afirmaciones, con las palabras en pantalla
8:36 Vuelta 2: las mismas afirmaciones en otro orden, más despacio
18:07 Vuelta 3: las mismas afirmaciones en otro orden, más despacio
28:36 Vuelta 4: las mismas afirmaciones en otro orden, más despacio
40:05 Vuelta 5: las mismas afirmaciones en otro orden, más despacio, la voz cada vez más baja
52:33 La frase de cierre y después solo las ondas en 432 Hz

Voz: sintética (ElevenLabs), una voz de mujer. Las afirmaciones las escribe NAOS en español. Se aceptan correcciones.

snippet.title: Skipping the Gym? Like a Peasant. (Funny Gym Motivation)
snippet.description:
Skipping the gym again? That's peasant behavior. Cella is sunk into the couch, hears "like a peasant," and takes it personally: up, gym bag, out the door. One squat later she's back on the floor. Then she gets up and goes again.

How do you go to the gym when you don't feel like it? Most people who keep going say the same thing: don't wait to feel motivated. Pack the bag, get out the door, and promise yourself just one exercise. One squat still counts as showing up.

A short cartoon about gym motivation for lazy days.

snippet.title: Cold Shower Challenge: Did You Hear What Cella Did?
snippet.description:
Cold shower challenge, neighborhood edition. Two neighbors gossip about Cella: she says she's built different. They say she owns a heated blanket. Cella hears every word, steps under the cold water, shivers, and stays.

Why would anyone take a cold shower on purpose? People do it as hormesis: a small stress your body adapts to. The point isn't comfort. It's choosing the harder option for a moment and staying anyway.

How long should a cold shower be? There's no single number. Most people start with a few seconds at the end of a warm shower and build up from there. It isn't for everyone: if you have a heart condition, ask a doctor first.
